 A Rio Arriba County jury has awarded $47 million to a man and his mother nearly four years after a commercial truck crash left him with traumatic brain injuries and a permanent need for round-the-clock care.
 The verdict, reached Friday in a Tierra Amarilla courtroom, followed a trial in the First Judicial District Court that centered on a head-on collision near Carlsbad between military veteran Austin Drewry and a commercial tanker truck. It is one of the largest jury awards in a nonfatal truck crash in New Mexico’s history.
 “I just want to say thank you to Rio Arriba County for listening to our stories and our case and really [being] in favor of Austin and giving him that justice that we have fought so hard for,” said Crystal Drewry, Austin Drewry’s mother.
 Austin Drewry, then-21 and an oilfield worker, was driving eastbound on N.M. 128 on a foggy night in November 2022 when a commercial truck traveling westbound collided with him head-on. The driver of the truck, who is not a defendant in the case, was employed by Pilot Thomas Logistics LLC, a fuel and lubricant company headquartered in Grapevine, Texas.
 Austin Drewry
 Courtesy photo 
 A spokesperson for the company did not respond to a request for comment.
 Crystal Drewry filed a lawsuit with her son’s court-appointed co-conservator against Pilot Thomas Logistics and subsidiary Maxum Petroleum Operating Co. — which both have a registered agent in Española — in 2024 in Rio Arriba County. The complaint alleged the truck driver was traveling too fast for the weather conditions and failed to recognize and respond to Austin Drewry’s vehicle.
 The driver, who was dismissed as a party in the case by Judge Francis Mathew, was traveling above the 55 mph speed limit and had previously been disciplined by Pilot Thomas Logistics for speeding, according to a transcript of a deposition of the driver.
 “If the driver would’ve just stopped for half a second more, hit the brakes for half a second more, slowed down like he’s supposed to do in the fog or get off the road in the fog, the crash would have never happened,” James Tawney, lead attorney for the plaintiffs, said in an interview. “It was literally split seconds of difference.”
 Attorneys for Pilot Thomas Logistics and Maxum Patroleum Operating Co. first offered to settle the case for $100,000 before it went to trial, Tawney said. The plaintiffs refused, hoping a jury would have “a little more compassion and understanding and empathy” for the gravity of the damages posed to Austin Drewry’s life, he said.
 “We knew we were going to try the case,” Tawney added.
 The Pilot Thomas Logistics truck that collided with Austin Drewry’s vehicle after the crash in November 2022. The accident left him with traumatic brain injuries and a permanent need for round-the-clock care.
 Courtesy photo 
 The crash caused extensive injuries to Drewry’s brain, spinal cord, bones and internal organs — and ultimately his incapacitation, according to the complaint. A veteran of the Louisiana National Guard, he was planning to return home to Mangham, La., to be with his family for Thanksgiving, but instead was transported from Carlsbad Medical Center to a trauma center in El Paso.
 Drewry coded — or suffered a life-threatening emergency — twice in 2023, The Ouachita Citizen in Louisiana reported last year.
 He is still bedridden and cannot talk or function on his own, Tawney said. A Facebook account called “ Austin’s Fight For Life ” remains active with updates on Drewry’s life and medical status.
 Crystal Drewry, who is her son’s full-time caregiver, said the financial award will give him “the things that he needs that he’s not been able to get.”
 “He will be taken care of even when I’m gone,” she said. “So, he’s getting a chance to live.”
 Tawney described the verdict as “justice for Austin and his mother.”
 “It signals that New Mexicans appreciate human life, and they understand that human life is worth something,” he said.
 Lily Alexander is a state accountability reporter for The New Mexican and Searchlight New Mexico, focusing on equity and transparency. Her position is part of the New Mexican Public Service Journalism Fund, and her stories are available to all readers without a paywall.
